title: Dunhuang: The Caves That Saved a Library

cards.h: A library hidden in a cliff
cards.b:
In 1900 a Daoist monk named Wang Yuanlu found a sealed room behind a wall in the Mogao Caves near Dunhuang, on the Silk Road in northwest China. Inside were tens of thousands of manuscripts, written over centuries.

The discovery changed what we know about Buddhism, Chinese history and the Silk Road. It is still one of the great finds of modern scholarship.

The Mogao Caves were carved from the cliffs from about 366 CE onward, according to tradition. Over the next thousand years monks, donors and artists painted murals and built statues. The caves became a major centre of Buddhist art.

Dunhuang sat where roads from China split into northern and southern routes across the Taklamakan desert. Merchants, monks and pilgrims all passed through.

The library cave, known as Cave 17, was sealed up around the 11th century. The reasons are unclear. Some think it was done to protect the texts from danger, others think the monks simply abandoned the site.

When Wang Yuanlu opened it in 1900, he found manuscripts in Chinese, Tibetan, Sanskrit, Uighur and other languages. Many were Buddhist scriptures, but there were also letters, contracts and popular songs.

The Diamond Sutra (868 CE)

One scroll found in the cave is a printed copy of the Diamond Sutra, dated 868 CE. It is the earliest dated printed book known, made with woodblocks and a colophon with the date.

It is now in the British Library, and it is often shown as a landmark in the history of print.
The timeline runs from the first caves to the modern collectors who carried the manuscripts away.

cards.h: Aurel Stein and the Western collectors
cards.b:
In 1907 the Hungarian-born British explorer Aurel Stein bought a large number of manuscripts from Wang. The following year the French scholar Paul Pelliot also collected many texts. Their works now sit in London, Paris, Beijing and other cities.

The purchases were controversial then and remain so now. Many Chinese scholars see the removals as a loss of national heritage, while others argue that the texts were preserved better in libraries abroad.

cards.h: Did Wang Yuanlu sell the treasures for a pittance?
cards.b:
A common story says that Wang sold the library for small sums and that he did not understand what he had. The image makes him a villain or a fool, and it is widely repeated.

Historians argue the story is partly true and partly unfair. Wang did sell texts for money, and he was not a scholar. But he also tried to protect the site and to report his find. The real picture of his choices is complex.

The Dunhuang texts include sutras, histories, medical texts, calendars and songs. They show the variety of life at a Silk Road city. Some texts give voices to ordinary people, such as merchants, women and soldiers.

Historians argue that the library is a snapshot of a border region, not a full picture of China. Its strange mix of texts is valuable precisely because it does not fit neatly into one tradition.

The Diamond Sutra was originally a Sanskrit text. The monk Kumarajiva, who came from the Silk Road city of Kucha, translated it into Chinese around 402 CE. That translation was copied and spread across East Asia.

The text is a Buddhist teaching about emptiness and illusion. Its message reached far beyond the caves and helped shape Chinese Buddhism.

The Dunhuang manuscripts were written in more than a dozen languages, including Tibetan, Uighur, Khotanese and Sogdian. They show the reach of Silk Road networks and the mixing of cultures in a border city.

The site is a UNESCO World Heritage Site today. Its caves and manuscripts show how a border town can hold the memory of an entire trade world.

The Diamond Sutra was a Sanskrit text from India. Its message came to China through monks and translators, and the Silk Road carried Indian Buddhist ideas across Central Asia. Dunhuang shows that link in paper and paint.

Indian monks, artists and teachers were part of the same world of exchange. The caves show Indian themes, such as stories of the Buddha, carried to China along the route.

Five things to remember
  1. The Mogao Caves near Dunhuang hold a sealed library.
  2. Wang Yuanlu found it in 1900.
  3. The Diamond Sutra printed in 868 is the earliest dated printed book known.
  4. Stein and Pelliot took many manuscripts abroad.
  5. The texts are in many languages, including Sanskrit and Tibetan.
Think about it
  • Who should own a heritage found in one country but written by many peoples?
  • What makes a text worth keeping?
